entities.name: Abolition of the Ottoman Caliphate
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Abolition of the Ottoman Caliphate (March 3, 1924) by the Grand National Assembly of Turkey under Mustafa Kemal Atatürk's leadership was one of the most symbolically momentous acts of the 20th century — ending an institution (the Caliphate of Islam, the political and religious leadership of the world's Sunni Muslim community) that had continued in various forms since the Prophet Muhammad's death in 632 CE, and marking a radical break with Islamic political tradition as the new Turkish Republic proclaimed itself a secular state separated from Islamic religious authority.

The Ottoman Caliphate had evolved from the early Arab caliphates through the Abbasid line; the Ottoman sultans claimed the caliphal title after conquering Egypt (1517), when the last Abbasid caliph in Cairo was said to have transferred the title to Sultan Selim I. By the 19th-20th centuries, the Ottoman caliphate had become a focus of pan-Islamic political movements and was used by Ottoman sultans (especially Abdul Hamid II) as a tool of soft power over Muslim populations worldwide — including British India, where 60 million Muslims lived.

Atatürk's abolition was the culminating step of his secularization program: the Sultanate had been abolished in 1922; Caliph Abdülmecid II was retained as a purely religious figure; but the caliphate was seen as an obstacle to modernization and a potential rallying point for political Islam. The abolition created a crisis in the global Muslim community — the Khilafat Movement in India (which had lobbied Britain to preserve the Ottoman Caliphate) collapsed; attempts to establish a new caliphate in Cairo and elsewhere failed; and the question of who holds legitimate Islamic political authority remains unresolved to the present.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Abolition of the Ottoman Caliphate (1924) — ending an institution of Islamic political authority continuous since 632 CE, creating a global Sunni leadership vacuum, inspiring the Khilafat Movement's collapse, and establishing Turkey's secular model — is one of the 20th century's most symbolically momentous acts with continuing reverberations in Islamic political thought.
